titre: Fazlur Khan makes Chicago's towers stand like hollow tubes
accroche: In 1965, to hold up a hundred stories against the wind, engineer Fazlur Khan makes a tower's entire facade work like a hollow tube.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1965, architect Bruce Graham and engineer Fazlur Khan, both at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill in Chicago, design the John Hancock Center: a hundred stories, a mix of offices and apartments, in the windy downtown on Lake Michigan. At that height, the problem is no longer carrying the building's weight vertically (any steel frame can do that) but resisting the horizontal push of the wind, which grows with every story. The usual method, a dense frame of columns and beams spread throughout the building, would require so much steel here that the lower floors would have almost no usable space left.

## The whole facade works as a single piece

Khan had already tested part of the solution two years earlier, on an apartment building in the same city, the DeWitt-Chestnut: instead of spreading the load-bearing columns throughout the floor plan, he packs them tightly around the building's perimeter alone, linked by rigid beams. The whole then behaves like a thin-walled tube anchored in the ground: a “framed tube.” For the Hancock Center, taller and more exposed, Khan goes further: on all four facades he adds a network of giant steel X-braces, visible from outside, which carry the push of the wind directly to the building's corners rather than distributing it through the whole structure. This “braced tube” frees the tower's interior, almost entirely clear of load-bearing columns, and requires only 145 kilograms of steel per square meter, against 206 for the Empire State Building, built forty years earlier with a conventional frame.

## What this shifts

Four years later, in 1973, Khan takes the same principle up again for the Sears Tower and pushes it further: instead of a single tube, he assembles nine, welded together into a “bundled tube” that makes the building the world's tallest for twenty-five years. The lesson holds beyond Chicago: it changes what a high-rise has to be in order to stand, no longer a solid frame but a shell that works as a whole. Almost every tower built since uses some variant of Khan's tube. The principle is even still being refined: in 2008, Khan's own heirs at SOM show that moving the central node of the Hancock Center's X-braces to three-quarters of the height of each module would have improved its material efficiency by about 10%, nearly forty years after construction.

repere.texte: Fazlur Khan first applies the framed tube principle to the DeWitt-Chestnut Building in Chicago, as early as 1963, then as a braced tube for the John Hancock Center (1965-1969), before assembling nine tubes for the Sears Tower in 1973, the world's tallest tower for twenty-five years.

carte.punch: Fazlur Khan made a hundred-story skyscraper stand like a hollow tube.
carte.idee: In 1965, engineer Fazlur Khan gives up the solid frame for the John Hancock Center: the entire facade works as a tube, reinforced with giant steel X-braces that carry the wind to the corners. Almost every tower built since uses a variant of his principle.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Perfecting Structure: From X-Braced Steel to Concrete and Back, SOM
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The firm that designed the John Hancock Center looks back on the legacy of Khan's braced tube and on its refinement forty years later.

quiz.question: Why does Fazlur Khan make the entire facade of the John Hancock Center work as a tube, rather than spreading columns throughout the building?
choix: Because concentrating the resistance on the perimeter frees up the interior of the floors and requires far less steel than a distributed frame
Because Chicago's soil, too soft, cannot bear the weight of interior columns over a hundred stories
Because Chicago's city hall imposed a building permit limiting the number of columns visible from the street
Because a tube uses less concrete than a conventional steel frame, which lowered the cost of the project
quiz.explication: Concentrating the load-bearing elements on the perimeter makes the entire facade work as a tube, which frees the floors of interior columns and requires only 145 kg of steel per m², against 206 for the Empire State Building; neither the soil, nor a building permit, nor concrete savings explain this choice, since the structure remains steel.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What innovation does Fazlur Khan first apply to the DeWitt-Chestnut Building in 1963?
choix: The framed tube, with load-bearing columns packed tightly around the building's perimeter alone
The braced tube, reinforced with giant steel X-braces visible on the facade
The bundled tube, assembling several tubes welded together
The floating foundation, which spreads the weight over a single mat slab
quiz_supplementaire.explication: At the DeWitt-Chestnut, Khan packs the load-bearing columns tightly around the building's perimeter alone, a framed tube; the braced tube, with its visible X-braces, appears only at the Hancock Center.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the 2008 re-analysis by SOM engineers show about the structure of the John Hancock Center?
choix: That the structure was undersized and needed reinforcement
That moving the node of the X-braces to three-quarters of the module's height would gain about 10% in efficiency
That the braced tube actually used more steel than the Empire State Building
That the tube principle only worked beyond a hundred stories
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2008 re-analysis shows that moving the central node of the X-braces to three-quarters of the height of each module would have improved its material efficiency by about 10%.
